clue.text: This Turner looks just the same upside down

parts.note: surface reading: a painting by J.M.W. Turner; setter's reading: anything that turns or spins

parts.words: looks just the same upside down
parts.note: surface reading: an abstract-looking canvas; setter's reading: in a down light, the word reads identically from bottom to top

explanation.surface: An art-lover remarks that one of J.M.W. Turner's paintings looks no different when hung upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner seems to be the painter, but it is just anything that turns; the down light reads the same from either end.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotator is a device or muscle that makes something revolve, so it is literally one that turns.

clue.text: Smackhead hallucinated and took off clothes

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only the start of smack is kept

parts.note: the head, or first letter, of smack
to trip is to hallucinate on drugs

explanation.surface: A heroin addict, out of their mind on drugs, strips naked.
explanation.walkthrough: Smackhead looks like one word for a heroin user, but it splits into smack's head, its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip is to remove one's garments, so having stripped means having undressed completely.

clue.text: Where you can vote for Cherie''s nearest and dearest?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the small screened stalls at a polling station
second meaning: Cherie Blair was born Cherie Booth, so her family share that surname

explanation.surface: A question about where Cherie Blair's loved ones go to cast their votes.
explanation.walkthrough: Cherie Blair, wife of the then Prime Minister Tony Blair, was born Cherie Booth; her relatives are therefore the Booths.
explanation.definitionFit: Voters mark their ballot papers in private polling stalls, and a family surnamed Booth are collectively the Booths.

clue.text: One add one? (Understand, it''s in double figures!)

parts.note: one plus one makes this number
slang: 'I dig' means I understand
taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzled sum: one plus one, and the exasperated answer that it has reached double figures.
explanation.walkthrough: The sum gives a number word, then dig and it follow; the answer itself describes numbers from ten to ninety-nine.
explanation.definitionFit: A number written with two numerals, from ten upward to ninety-nine, sits in the range called double figures.

clue.text: Suture lacerated womb

indicators.note: something lacerated is torn apart, so the letters of the word before it are ripped and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A surgical stitch has been torn in the womb after an operation.
explanation.definitionFit: Uterus is the anatomical term for the organ in which a baby develops before birth.

clue.text: Cut leg badly below front edge of tibia

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting one piece below another means writing it after

parts.note: the shin is the front edge of the tibia, the shinbone

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters of leg come out in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A patient has a nasty gash on the leg, just under the sharp ridge of the shinbone.
explanation.walkthrough: Cut looks like an injury, but it is a hairstyle; a shingle is a short tapered women's haircut popular in the 1920s.
explanation.definitionFit: A shingle is a style of haircut, short and tapering at the nape, so it is a kind of cut.

clue.text: Bridge is a card game

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a floating bridge supported on boats or floats
second meaning: the British name for blackjack or twenty-one

explanation.surface: A simple statement that bridge is a card game, which is true.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge reads as the card game, but here it is a structure across water.
explanation.definitionFit: A pontoon is a temporary bridge laid on floats, and pontoon is also the British name for blackjack.

clue.text: On edge, start to tremble with dreadful tic. Why?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only the opening of tremble is used

parts.note: the first letter of tremble

indicators.note: dreadful suggests something in a terrible state, so the following letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A nervous person, trembling with a terrible facial tic, wonders why it is happening.
explanation.definitionFit: Being twitchy means jumpy and nervous, which is what being on edge means.

clue.text: Revive production of "Cats"? It sure takes energy

indicators.note: a new production of a show is a fresh staging, so these letters are put together again in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: A theatre critic wonders whether reviving the musical Cats would take a lot of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Revive looks like it belongs with the theatre talk, but it is the definition; the fodder is the show's name, then 'It sure', plus E.
explanation.definitionFit: To resuscitate someone is to bring them back to consciousness or life, which is to revive them.

clue.text: It's wrong to pursue pathetic pervert

indicators.note: to pursue is to follow behind, so this piece comes after the next one

parts.note: sad in its slang sense of pathetic or pitiful

indicators.note: something wrong is not in its proper state, so the letters are put out of their order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A moral judgement that it is wrong to chase after some pitiful deviant.
explanation.definitionFit: A sadist takes sexual pleasure in inflicting pain, so is a kind of sexual deviant, or pervert.

clue.text: Permanent end to upper-class clique

parts.note: taken as written
U is the old label for upper-class usage
a ring is a closed group of people, such as a spy ring

explanation.surface: A call to abolish the exclusive cliques of the upper classes once and for all.
explanation.walkthrough: U and non-U were labels for upper-class and middle-class speech in 1950s Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enduring lasts a very long time without fading, which is close to permanent.

clue.text: Mowlam returns in very quiet show of importance

indicators.note: returning means going back the way one came, so the name is read from right to left
in places one piece inside another, here within the notation for very quiet

parts.note: pp, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very quietly
Mo Mowlam was Labour's Northern Ireland Secretary, always known as Mo

explanation.surface: Mo Mowlam makes a quiet comeback, which turns out to be a display of her importance.
explanation.walkthrough: Mowlam stands for her first name, Mo, a popular Labour politician of the late 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomp is ceremonial splendour, a grand display put on to show how important someone is.

clue.text: Hugs silly German awkwardly, without much energy

indicators.note: done awkwardly means clumsily, so these letters are fumbled into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
G is the abbreviation for German

explanation.surface: Someone clumsily and listlessly embraces a foolish German.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something sluggishly means doing it slowly and lethargically, with little vigour or energy.

clue.text: Instruction bewildered idiot fiance

indicators.note: someone bewildered is confused, so the letters that follow are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone must give instructions to a hopelessly confused and foolish husband-to-be.
explanation.definitionFit: Edification is moral or intellectual improvement through teaching, so it amounts to instruction.

clue.text: Fellow takes on 50 frenzied houris — what a gesture!

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow

indicators.note: something frenzied is wild and out of control, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A man takes on fifty wild nymphs of paradise, and what a grand gesture that is.
explanation.walkthrough: Houris are the beautiful maidens of the Islamic paradise.
explanation.definitionFit: A flourish is a showy, sweeping movement of the hand or body, a kind of theatrical gesture.

clue.text: "Spectator" — a Guardian Media Group publication?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a person who watches
second meaning: the Sunday newspaper owned by the group behind the Guardian

explanation.walkthrough: The Spectator is itself a British magazine, so the quotation marks suggest a title; here it simply means a watcher.
explanation.definitionFit: An observer is someone who watches events, and The Observer is the Sunday sister paper of the Guardian.

clue.text: Opens "Sunday People" first and reads

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for Sunday

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: the first letter of people
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone opens the Sunday People newspaper before anything else and reads it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sunday People is a British tabloid newspaper; the quotation marks hide two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To spread something is to open it out, as one spreads a map or a newspaper.

clue.text: Tory has single comfort

parts.note: Con is the abbreviation for Conservative, a Tory
sole means only or single

explanation.surface: A lonely Conservative politician finds comfort in being on their own.
explanation.definitionFit: To console someone is to offer them solace in grief or disappointment, so to comfort them.

clue.text: For example, Campbell's fixer, taking party to centre first, then to the right

definitions.text: For example, Campbell's fixer, taking party to centre first, then to the right

parts.note: surface reading: someone who sorts things out for a man called Campbell

parts.words: taking party to centre first, then to the right
parts.note: setter's reading: Alastair Campbell, Tony Blair's press chief, steered the image of the Labour Party towards the political centre and beyond

explanation.walkthrough: Alastair Campbell was Tony Blair's communications director, famed for managing New Labour's media message as it moved from left to centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A media adviser who presents a party's policies in the most favourable light is known by this term, and Campbell was the archetype.

clue.text: Refusal to dole out pasta

parts.note: no is a refusal

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters of the word before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to hand out portions of pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: Dole out looks like a phrasal verb meaning to hand out, but the out is the jumble signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Noodles are long thin strips of pasta, so a single noodle is a piece of pasta.

clue.text: Conservatism''s morally just claims

parts.note: the Right is the conservative wing of politics
the possessive ending, taken as written

explanation.surface: A statement that conservatism's claims are morally just.
explanation.definitionFit: Rights are entitlements that a person may justly claim, on moral or legal grounds.

clue.text: Gunned down in Paris hotel

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the following words, running across them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Paris and the start of hotel

explanation.surface: Someone is gunned down in a hotel in Paris, like a thriller scene.
explanation.definitionFit: To be shot is to be hit with a bullet, so someone shot has been gunned down.

clue.text: Clinton is one bad actor after initially denying embracing Monica

indicators.note: after says the rearranged piece is written following the initial letters
initially points to the first letters of the words that follow it

parts.note: the first letters of denying, embracing and Monica

indicators.note: bad means faulty, so the word after it is put into a wrong order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Bill Clinton is a poor performer when he denies having embraced Monica Lewinsky.
explanation.walkthrough: Initially seems to belong to denying alone, but it takes the first letter of all three words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill Clinton was a President from the American Democratic Party, so he is one of its members.

clue.text: Finally realising Onassis is hard and showy

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the last letter of realising
Aristotle Onassis, the Greek shipping tycoon, was known as Ari; Ari is becomes Ari's
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Someone finally realises that the tycoon Onassis is a tough and flashy man.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb is folds into the name as an apostrophe-s, as in Ari's.
explanation.definitionFit: Garish means gaudy and over-bright, the look of something designed to be showy.

clue.text: Worship Lise before I do?

indicators.note: before marks the moment in a wedding when the vow is spoken, so the vow comes first and the name follows

parts.note: taken as written: the wedding vow
taken as written

explanation.surface: A groom wonders whether he should adore his bride Lise even before saying his vows.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts Lise first, but the pieces join as the vow followed by the name, as a groom would say it to her.
explanation.definitionFit: To idolise someone is to admire them excessively, treating them like an idol, which is to worship them.

clue.text: Tower is precipitous and partly leaning

parts.note: steep means sharply sloping, like a precipice

indicators.note: partly means only a portion of the word that follows is used

parts.note: the opening two letters of leaning

explanation.surface: A church tower is described as dangerously high and partly tilting over.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is the tall pointed structure rising above a church, a kind of tower.
